title: Episode 20: Accessibility Standards Reference
description: WCAG 2.2, ARIA roles, and the PR accessibility checklist.
concepts: What WCAG is: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
The four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust
Key WCAG 2.2 success criteria relevant to development
What ARIA is: Accessible Rich Internet Applications
Common ARIA roles: button, dialog, navigation, landmark, live region
The PR accessibility checklist: what to check before merging
How to apply accessibility standards in code review
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. This time, we’re building a practical reference in audio form: the accessibility standards that show up when you use GitHub, review pull requests, write docs, or contribute code to the web.

[JAMIE]
So this is the episode for the moment when somebody comments, “This may fail WCAG 1.4.3,” and you think, I know that matters, but I need help decoding it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Think of this as a working guide, not a memorization exercise. It’s a companion to open source collaboration and also very relevant when you work in VS Code or inspect web interfaces. And if you want the canonical standards, the authoritative references are the W3C documents for WCAG 2.2 and WAI-ARIA 1.2.

[JAMIE]
Before we dive in, can we set expectations? Are learners supposed to memorize criterion numbers?

[ALEX]
No. You should recognize the big ideas, know the common trouble spots, and know where to look things up. This appendix is a lookup reference, and this episode turns that into a conversation you can carry into reviews and bug reports.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let’s orient the map. The material moves through the four WCAG principles, conformance levels, commonly encountered success criteria, ARIA basics, landmark roles, common ARIA patterns, how standards apply to GitHub contributions, testing, a pull request checklist, and official references.

[JAMIE]
That’s helpful, because accessibility standards can feel like a giant wall of acronyms unless you know the structure.

[ALEX]
Right. And the structure starts with WCAG.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
WCAG stands for Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. Version 2.2 is organized around four principles often remembered with the mnemonic POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust.

[JAMIE]
Let’s make each one concrete.

[ALEX]
Perceivable means information must be available in ways users can actually perceive. If an image has no alt text, a screen reader user may get nothing meaningful. That’s a perceivability failure.

[JAMIE]
So the content exists visually, but not accessibly.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Operable means people must be able to use the interface. If a control only works on hover, keyboard users may be blocked. That’s an operability failure.

[JAMIE]
Understandable sounds like both wording and behavior.

[ALEX]
Yes. If a form says only “Invalid input” but never explains what is wrong, the system is not understandable enough. Users need clear labels, instructions, and error explanations.

[JAMIE]
And Robust?

[ALEX]
Robust means content has to work with assistive technologies and across different user agents. A custom widget with JavaScript but no proper semantics may leave a screen reader unable to identify what it is, what state it’s in, or how to interact with it.

[JAMIE]
So every WCAG success criterion belongs to one of those four buckets.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That’s the high-level index for everything else.

[JAMIE]
The learning cards in the source also had audience-specific advice. Can we fold that in?

[ALEX]
Absolutely. For screen reader users: remember POUR as your fast review lens, know that many projects target WCAG 2.2 AA, and when someone cites a number like 1.4.3, the WCAG quick reference is searchable by criterion number.

For low-vision users: contrast criteria like 1.4.3 for text contrast and 1.4.11 for non-text contrast are especially relevant day to day. If tables are hard to read in plain Markdown, use larger editor text or Markdown preview. And when checking contrast with a tool like WebAIM’s contrast checker, use your usual zoom level so you stay in your normal workflow.

For sighted users: the quick mental shortcut is to connect each principle to a typical failure. Also, pay attention to conformance levels in tables, because AA is usually the practical target. And the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide is worth bookmarking for real pattern examples.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
That leads nicely to conformance levels. What do A, AA, and AAA really mean in practice?

[ALEX]
Level A is the baseline. It removes the most severe barriers and is often the minimum legal floor in many contexts. Level AA goes further and removes significant barriers; it’s the common compliance target for WCAG 2.2, for many enterprise and government contexts, and it aligns with GitHub’s accessibility commitments. Level AAA is the highest level, but it is not generally required across the board and is applied where feasible.

[JAMIE]
So if I’m contributing to an open source web project and I want to use the standard most reviewers will recognize, I should usually reference WCAG 2.2 AA.

[ALEX]
Yes. That is the safest default unless the project says otherwise.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let’s cover the success criteria you are most likely to encounter in web contributions.

[JAMIE]
And maybe translate them into things you can notice in a pull request.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[ALEX]
Under Perceivable, one of the biggest is 1.1.1 Non-text Content. Images, icons, and other non-text content need text alternatives, whether that’s alt text, an accessible name, or another appropriate text equivalent.

[JAMIE]
So a meaningful icon-only button with no label is a problem.

[ALEX]
Yes. Next is 1.3.1 Info and Relationships. If structure is communicated visually with headings, lists, or tables, that structure also needs to exist programmatically.

[JAMIE]
Meaning you can’t just make text look like a heading with bold styling.

[ALEX]
Right. Use real headings. Then 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence: the reading order should still make sense, even if CSS is removed or layout shifts. That matters because assistive tech often follows DOM order, not just visual layout.

[JAMIE]
And 1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics says don’t rely only on things like “click the green button on the right.”

[ALEX]
Exactly. Instructions should not depend solely on color, shape, sound, or position. 1.4.1 Use of Color continues that theme: color alone cannot carry the information.

[JAMIE]
Then the contrast criteria.

[ALEX]
Yes. 1.4.3 Contrast Minimum requires at least a 4.5 to 1 contrast ratio for normal text, or 3 to 1 for large text. 1.4.4 Resize Text means text can be resized to 200 percent without losing content or functionality. 1.4.10 Reflow means content should work at 400 percent zoom without forcing horizontal scrolling in typical cases. And 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast requires UI components and graphical objects to meet at least 3 to 1 contrast.

[JAMIE]
That one gets missed a lot, right? People think only body text contrast matters.

[ALEX]
Yes. Focus indicators, buttons, form boundaries, icons, and other UI elements matter too.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Under Operable, start with 2.1.1 Keyboard. All functionality must be available by keyboard alone.

[JAMIE]
Which means if I can only trigger a control with a mouse, that’s a failure.

[ALEX]
Correct. Then 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap: once focus enters a component, the user must be able to move focus away. A modal, menu, or custom widget cannot trap someone indefinitely.

[JAMIE]
And 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks is where skip links come in.

[ALEX]
Yes. Repeated navigation should be skippable. 2.4.2 Page Titled means pages need descriptive titles. 2.4.3 Focus Order means keyboard focus should proceed logically. 2.4.4 Link Purpose means link text should say where it goes or what it does.

[JAMIE]
So “click here” and “read more” are often weak if they’re ambiguous out of context.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then 2.4.6 Headings and Labels says headings and labels should describe topic or purpose. 2.4.7 Focus Visible requires a visible focus indicator for keyboard users. 2.4.11 Focus Appearance, which is new in WCAG 2.2, raises the bar by requiring minimum size and contrast for that focus indicator.

[JAMIE]
That’s a good example of standards evolving from “there is some focus” to “the focus has to be meaningfully perceivable.”

[ALEX]
Well put. And 2.5.3 Label in Name matters especially for speech input and consistency. If a control visibly says “Submit order,” the accessible name should contain that visible text, not something unrelated like “Confirm purchase now.”

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Under Understandable, 3.1.1 Language of Page says the page language must be identified, usually with the HTML lang attribute. 3.2.1 On Focus means merely receiving focus should not trigger a surprising context change. 3.2.2 On Input says changing a setting should not unexpectedly launch something or move the user somewhere else unless they were warned.

[JAMIE]
So just tabbing into a field shouldn’t open a new page, and selecting an option shouldn’t suddenly submit a form without clear expectation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then 3.3.1 Error Identification says input errors need to be identified and described in text. 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions means forms need labels or instructions where input is required. And 3.3.3 Error Suggestion says that when possible, users should be told how to correct the issue, not merely that something went wrong.

[JAMIE]
That’s a subtle but important distinction: “invalid input” versus “password must be at least twelve characters.”

[ALEX]
Yes. Good accessible design reduces guesswork.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Under Robust, 4.1.1 Parsing means markup should not contain errors that break assistive technology interpretation. 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value says UI components need accessible names, semantic roles, and states that can be determined programmatically. And 4.1.3 Status Messages says updates like “item added” or “saved successfully” should be announced without moving focus.

[JAMIE]
That last one connects directly to live regions and polite announcements.

[ALEX]
Exactly, and we’ll get there shortly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now for the other big acronym: ARIA.

[ALEX]
ARIA stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications. It helps when native HTML cannot fully express a complex interface. But it’s not a replacement for semantic HTML. It fills gaps.

[JAMIE]
And the source breaks ARIA into three categories.

[ALEX]
Yes. Roles say what something is: button, dialog, tab. States describe changing conditions: expanded, checked, disabled. Properties describe characteristics or relationships: labels, descriptions, requiredness, and so on.

[JAMIE]
Can you give quick examples?

[ALEX]
Sure. A custom trigger might use role equals button. An accordion header may expose aria-expanded true or false. A close control might use aria-label equals Close dialog. An input may point to helper text with aria-describedby.

[JAMIE]
What are the main rules people should remember?

[ALEX]
Three big ones. First: do not use ARIA when native HTML already works. If you can use a real button, use a real button. Second: if you do create an interactive ARIA widget, it must be keyboard operable. A div with role button is not enough; you also need keyboard handling, focusability, and expected behavior. Third: ARIA affects the accessibility tree, not appearance or behavior. It changes what assistive technologies can understand, but it does not magically add visuals or interaction logic.

[JAMIE]
So ARIA can describe, but not fully build.

[ALEX]
Perfectly said.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
A particularly important ARIA topic is landmark roles. These let screen reader users jump quickly among major page regions.

[JAMIE]
And that’s very relevant on large sites like GitHub.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Common landmarks include banner for a site-wide header, navigation for nav links, main for primary page content, complementary for supporting side content, contentinfo for footer-like site information, search for search regions, and form when a form region needs landmark semantics.

[JAMIE]
And often there are native HTML equivalents, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. Header, nav, main, aside, footer, search-related structures, and forms often provide or imply these semantics depending on usage. The broader lesson is: prefer semantic HTML first, and understand landmarks as navigation points for assistive tech.

[JAMIE]
The source also notes practical navigation commands.

[ALEX]
Right. Screen reader users often jump by landmarks using commands like D in NVDA or JAWS, or the Rotor in VoiceOver. That’s one reason clear page regions matter so much.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s make ARIA more concrete with patterns people actually implement.

[ALEX]
Good idea. One pattern is the accessible button when a real button cannot be used.

[JAMIE]
Which is not the preferred choice.

[ALEX]
Correct. Preferred is always the real button element. But if you inherit a difficult codebase or truly cannot use button, the substitute needs at minimum button semantics, keyboard focus, and activation with Enter and Space. It also needs a clear accessible name.

[JAMIE]
So the lesson is less “here’s a cool div trick” and more “if you must do this, you inherit several responsibilities.”

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[ALEX]
Another pattern is an accessible form field with an error. A form control needs a proper label, and if there is an error, that error should be described in text, associated with the field, and ideally exposed in a way assistive technologies can announce. If the field is invalid, state should be programmatically represented, often with something like aria-invalid, plus a descriptive error message connected through an accessible relationship such as aria-describedby.

[JAMIE]
And that matches the WCAG requirements we talked about: error identification, labels or instructions, and error suggestions.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[ALEX]
Then there are live region status announcements. This is where 4.1.3 Status Messages often shows up. When something changes dynamically, like “settings saved” or “issue created,” users of assistive tech should be informed without having focus yanked away. Live regions provide that channel.

[JAMIE]
Usually with polite announcements unless it’s urgent.

[ALEX]
Yes. Use urgency carefully. The goal is to inform, not overwhelm.

[ALEX]
And finally, expandable sections, like accordions or disclosure widgets. The trigger should communicate whether the section is expanded or collapsed, usually through an expandable state, and the control should be keyboard operable, clearly labeled, and logically connected to the content it reveals.

[JAMIE]
Which is why a native details and summary pattern can sometimes be the best answer.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Native elements reduce the amount you have to recreate.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let’s bring this back to GitHub contributions, because that’s where learners need to apply the standards.

[ALEX]
Yes. There are three recurring situations here: filing an accessibility bug, reviewing a pull request for accessibility, and writing accessible documentation.

[JAMIE]
Start with bug reports.

[ALEX]
When filing an accessibility bug, be specific and standard-aware. Describe the user impact, the exact steps to reproduce, the environment if relevant, and the observed behavior. Then, where possible, connect it to a WCAG criterion. For example, instead of saying “the form is inaccessible,” say “the submit control has no accessible name, which affects screen reader users and may fail WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value.”

[JAMIE]
That gives maintainers something actionable rather than just alarming.

[ALEX]
Exactly. If it’s a contrast issue, cite the ratio and likely criterion. If it’s keyboard access, mention the exact key path that fails. If it’s a missing status announcement, explain what happened and what was not announced.

[JAMIE]
How about pull request review?

[ALEX]
Reviewing a PR for accessibility means checking the common standards we covered against the actual user experience. Ask: Are names, labels, and roles present? Is everything keyboard operable? Is focus visible and logical? Are headings meaningful? Does link text make sense? Do errors identify the problem and suggest correction? Are dynamic updates announced? Does zoom or reflow break the interface? Is color doing too much work by itself?

[JAMIE]
So you can review both code and behavior.

[ALEX]
Yes. Sometimes the markup looks fine until you actually tab through it or use a screen reader.

[JAMIE]
And writing accessible documentation?

[ALEX]
That matters more than many contributors realize. Use real heading structure, descriptive link text, meaningful alt text for informative images, and tables only when data is truly tabular. Avoid instructions based only on color or screen position. If a process depends on visuals, describe the nonvisual cues too. And when writing for GitHub issues, READMEs, or contributor guides, clarity is accessibility.

[JAMIE]
That includes administrative content too, right? Not just app UI.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Documentation, checklists, issue templates, contributing guides, and changelog notes are all part of an accessible workflow.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Testing is the other huge theme. The appendix makes a strong point that automated tools only catch part of the problem.

[ALEX]
Yes. Automated tools are useful, but they typically catch only about thirty to forty percent of issues. They’re great for finding missing alt text, some contrast failures, certain form labeling problems, missing landmarks, some ARIA misuse, and structural issues.

[JAMIE]
But they can’t tell the whole story.

[ALEX]
Exactly. They usually cannot judge whether alt text is meaningful, whether focus order truly makes sense, whether instructions are understandable, whether the reading order is coherent, whether a custom interaction is usable, or whether documentation is actually clear.

[JAMIE]
So manual testing catches the rest.

[ALEX]
Right. Manual testing should include keyboard-only testing, checking focus visibility and order, zoom and reflow testing, reviewing with a screen reader when possible, inspecting headings and landmarks, confirming link purpose, and trying forms with real error states.

[JAMIE]
Can we include the learning-card style guidance here too?

[ALEX]
Yes. For testing against standards, the mindset is: use automation first for broad detection, then manual testing for human judgment and interaction quality. If you’re a screen reader user, use landmarks, headings, and form navigation commands to evaluate structure efficiently. If you’re a low-vision tester, zoom and contrast checks are essential, not optional. If you’re a sighted keyboard tester, pay special attention to visible focus, logical tab order, and whether interactive elements expose their purpose without relying on a mouse.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let’s compress that into a fast pull request checklist.

[JAMIE]
The kind of thing you can mentally run before approving.

[ALEX]
Exactly. In a PR, check:

Are images and icon-only controls given meaningful text alternatives?
Are headings, lists, and tables semantically correct?
Does the reading order make sense?
Are instructions independent of color and position?
Is text contrast sufficient, and do UI elements meet non-text contrast needs?
Can everything be used with a keyboard?
Is there any keyboard trap?
Is focus order logical and focus indication clearly visible?
Do page titles, headings, labels, and links describe purpose well?
Does the accessible name contain the visible label where needed?
Are language, labels, instructions, and error messages present and clear?
Do error messages identify the issue and suggest a fix?
Do components expose name, role, and value correctly?
Are status messages announced without stealing focus?
If ARIA is used, is it necessary, and is the widget fully keyboard operable?

[JAMIE]
That’s a great practical translation of the standards into review behavior.

[ALEX]
That’s the goal. Standards should guide contribution decisions, not just sit in a reference document.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, what should learners treat as the official source of truth?

[ALEX]
For WCAG, use the W3C WCAG 2.2 specification and the W3C WCAG overview and quick reference materials. For ARIA, use WAI-ARIA 1.2 and the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide. For implementation help and examples, WAI tutorials are excellent. And for platform-specific context, GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog can help you track product behavior and documentation changes.

[JAMIE]
So if a project debate starts, “I read a blog post that said…,” you can ground the conversation in W3C and primary documentation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The appendix also included an authoritative source map by section, and the big idea there is simple: use official standards and official implementation guides whenever possible.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let me try a final summary without turning this into a shallow recap. WCAG gives us the four-part mental model: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. Most real-world contribution work targets WCAG 2.2 AA. The success criteria we’ll see most often involve text alternatives, semantic structure, contrast, zoom, keyboard access, focus behavior, clear labels and errors, and programmatic name-role-value support. ARIA helps with complex widgets, but native HTML is preferred. Landmarks and common patterns matter because they shape real navigation for assistive tech. And accessibility testing has to combine automation with manual checks.

[ALEX]
That’s excellent. And I’d add one final contributor mindset: when you file issues, review pull requests, or write documentation, try to name both the user impact and the likely standard involved. That combination makes you much more effective in collaborative accessibility work.

[JAMIE]
In other words, not just “this is broken,” but “this blocks keyboard users,” or “this status change is not announced,” or “this may fail WCAG 4.1.3.”

[ALEX]
Exactly. Precision helps teams fix real barriers.

[JAMIE]
And it helps learners grow from “I know accessibility matters” to “I can participate in accessibility review with confidence.”

[ALEX]
Well said.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
That’s it for this reference conversation. Keep the standards close, use them as tools rather than trivia, and let them shape how you contribute on GitHub and beyond.

# Appendix M: Accessibility Standards Reference > > **Listen to Episode 20:** [Accessibility Standards Reference](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned. > **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 08: Open Source Culture](08-open-source-culture.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 12](12-vscode-accessibility.md) > > **Authoritative source:** [W3C WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) | [WAI-ARIA 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/) ## WCAG, ARIA, and What They Mean for Your Contributions > This appendix gives you a working understanding of the accessibility standards that govern the web, GitHub's interface, and the projects you will contribute to. You do not need to memorize these - use this as a lookup when a PR review mentions a specific standard or success criterion. ## Table of Contents 1. [WCAG 2.2 - The Four Principles](#1-wcag-22---the-four-principles) 2. [Conformance Levels: A, AA, AAA](#2-conformance-levels-a-aa-aaa) 3. [Key Success Criteria for Web Contributions](#3-key-success-criteria-for-web-contributions) 4. [ARIA - Roles, States, and Properties](#4-aria---roles-states-and-properties) 5. [ARIA Landmark Roles](#5-aria-landmark-roles) 6. [Common ARIA Patterns](#6-common-aria-patterns) 7. [How Standards Apply to GitHub Contributions](#7-how-standards-apply-to-github-contributions) 8. [Testing Against Standards](#8-testing-against-standards) 9. [Quick Reference: What to Check in a PR](#9-quick-reference-what-to-check-in-a-pr) 10. [Official References](#10-official-references) ## 1. WCAG 2.2 - The Four Principles WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is organized around four principles, often abbreviated **POUR**: | Principle | Meaning | Example Failure | | ----------- | --------- | ----------------- | | **Perceivable** | Information must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive | An image with no alt text - a screen reader user gets nothing | | **Operable** | UI components and navigation must be operable | A button that only works on hover - keyboard users cannot activate it | | **Understandable** | Information and operation must be understandable | An error message that says "Invalid input" with no explanation of what is wrong | | **Robust** | Content must be robust enough to be interpreted by assistive technologies | Custom JavaScript widgets with no ARIA roles - screen readers cannot determine what they are | Every WCAG success criterion belongs to one of these four principles. ### Learning Cards: WCAG Overview
Screen reader users - WCAG is organized around four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust (POUR) — use this mnemonic when reviewing any PR - Most projects target WCAG 2.2 AA — when a reviewer cites a criterion number like 1.4.3, search the tables in Section 3 of this appendix - The WCAG Quick Reference (Section 10) is a filterable web page — use your screen reader's find command to jump to any criterion number
Low vision users - The tables in this appendix use pipe-delimited Markdown — increase your editor font size or use a Markdown preview for cleaner column alignment - WCAG 1.4.3 (contrast) and 1.4.11 (non-text contrast) are the criteria most relevant to your daily experience — bookmark them - When checking contrast ratios, use the WebAIM Contrast Checker link in Section 10 with your browser zoom set to your preferred level
Sighted users - The POUR table in this section is your one-glance cheat sheet — scan the Example Failure column to see what each principle looks like when violated - Conformance level badges (A, AA, AAA) appear in the Level column of the Section 3 tables — AA rows are your primary targets - Bookmark the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide link in Section 10 for live interactive pattern demos
## 2. Conformance Levels: A, AA, AAA | Level | Requirement | Who targets this | | ------- | ------------- | ----------------- | | **A** | Minimum accessibility - the baseline that removes the most severe barriers | Required by most accessibility laws | | **AA** | Enhanced accessibility - removes significant barriers | Required by WCAG 2.2 compliance targets, most government and enterprise standards, GitHub's own accessibility commitment | | **AAA** | Highest level - removes remaining barriers for the most niche cases | Not universally required; applied where feasible | Most open source projects, and GitHub itself, target **WCAG 2.2 AA** compliance. When you file an accessibility bug or review a PR, AA is the standard to reference. ## 3. Key Success Criteria for Web Contributions These are the criteria you will most commonly encounter when contributing to web projects or reviewing GitHub interface changes. ### Perceivable | Criterion | Level | What It Requires | | ----------- | ------- | ----------------- | | **1.1.1 Non-text Content** | A | All images, icons, and non-text content have a text alternative (`alt` attribute, `aria-label`, etc.) | | **1.3.1 Info and Relationships** | A | Structure conveyed visually (headings, lists, tables) is also conveyed programmatically | | **1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence** | A | Reading order makes sense when CSS is removed | | **1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics** | A | Instructions do not rely solely on shape, color, or position ("click the green button" fails this) | | **1.4.1 Use of Color** | A | Color is not the only means of conveying information | | **1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)** | AA | Text has at least 4.5:1 contrast ratio against its background (3:1 for large text) | | **1.4.4 Resize Text** | AA | Text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or function | | **1.4.10 Reflow** | AA | Content reflows at 400% zoom without horizontal scrolling | | **1.4.11 Non-text Contrast** | AA | UI components and graphical objects have at least 3:1 contrast | ### Operable | Criterion | Level | What It Requires | | ----------- | ------- | ----------------- | | **2.1.1 Keyboard** | A | All functionality is available via keyboard | | **2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap** | A | Keyboard focus can always be moved away from any component | | **2.4.1 Bypass Blocks** | A | A mechanism to skip repeated navigation (skip link) | | **2.4.2 Page Titled** | A | Pages have descriptive titles | | **2.4.3 Focus Order** | A | Focus follows a logical sequence | | **2.4.4 Link Purpose** | A | Link text describes the destination ("Read more about issues" not just "Read more") | | **2.4.6 Headings and Labels** | AA | Headings and labels describe their topic or purpose | | **2.4.7 Focus Visible** | AA | Keyboard focus indicator is visible | | **2.4.11 Focus Appearance** | AA *(2.2 new)* | Focus indicator meets minimum size and contrast | | **2.5.3 Label in Name** | A | For controls with visible labels, the accessible name contains the visible text | ### Understandable | Criterion | Level | What It Requires | | ----------- | ------- | ----------------- | | **3.1.1 Language of Page** | A | The default language is identified in the HTML (`lang` attribute) | | **3.2.1 On Focus** | A | Receiving focus does not trigger unexpected context changes | | **3.2.2 On Input** | A | Changing a setting does not cause unexpected changes unless the user is warned | | **3.3.1 Error Identification** | A | Input errors are identified and described in text | | **3.3.2 Labels or Instructions** | A | Labels or instructions are provided when user input is required | | **3.3.3 Error Suggestion** | AA | When an error is detected, suggestions for correction are provided | ### Robust | Criterion | Level | What It Requires | | ----------- | ------- | ----------------- | | **4.1.1 Parsing** | A | HTML/markup does not have errors that break AT interpretation | | **4.1.2 Name, Role, Value** | A | All UI components have accessible names, roles, and states that can be programmatically determined | | **4.1.3 Status Messages** | AA | Status messages (e.g. "item added to cart") are announced without receiving focus | ## 4. ARIA - Roles, States, and Properties WAI-ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) fills the gap between what HTML natively expresses and what complex interactive widgets require. ### Three categories | Category | Purpose | Examples | | ---------- | --------- | --------- | | **Roles** | What the element *is* | `role="button"`, `role="dialog"`, `role="tab"` | | **States** | Current condition (can change) | `aria-expanded="false"`, `aria-checked="true"`, `aria-disabled="true"` | | **Properties** | Stable characteristics | `aria-label="Close dialog"`, `aria-required="true"`, `aria-describedby="hint-text"` | ### Important rules 1. **Don't use ARIA if native HTML suffices.** A `
...content...
``` When expanded: set `aria-expanded="true"` and remove the `hidden` attribute. ## 7. This makes the bug actionable: > **Bad:** "The button isn't accessible." > **Good:** "The 'Subscribe' button has no visible focus indicator, failing WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA). currentFacts: The Accessibility Agents collection grows over time. Refer to it as a living catalog rather than asserting a fixed count of agents.
Challenge 15 (Discover Accessibility Agents) is browse-first. Learners are not required to fork the accessibility-agents repository to complete it.
Completing Challenge 15 unlocks Challenge 16 (Capstone Project) plus Bonus Challenges A through E. The bonus challenges are a structured unlock path, not "things to do if you finish early".

Challenge 16 is titled "Capstone Project". It accepts contributions to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or any other meaningful repository. Review-ready drafts and contribution plans are valid evidence of completion.
The Learning Room repository is where Day 1 contributions happen (issue, branch, commit, pull request, merge). It is provisioned per learner.
Hosts are Alex (warm expert) and Jamie (curious co-host who asks the questions learners hesitate to ask). They are colleagues, not teacher and student.

[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
